'''Harald Anton Enge''' (September 28, 1920, [[Fauske Municipality]], [[Nordland]], Norway<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref> – April 14, 2008, [[Middlesex County, Massachusetts]])<ref name=obitBostonGlobe>{{cite news|url=https://archive.boston.com/bostonglobe/obituaries/articles/2008/05/01/harald_enge_87_physicist_pillar_at_mit/|newspaper=The Boston Globe|title=Harald Enge, 87, physicist, pillar at MIT|author=Collette, Matt|date=May 1, 2008}}</ref> was a Norwegian-American experimental nuclear physicist and inventor of instrumentation used in nuclear physics. He is known for the Enge split-pole spectrograph, which became a standard instrument of nuclear physics research.<ref name=PT1984>{{cite journal|title=Bonner prize for nuclear physics to Harald A. Enge|journal=Physics Today|volume=37|issue=5|page=97|year=1984|doi=10.1063/1.2916257}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|year=2017|chapter=''The TUNL Enge split-pole spectrograph: A facility entirely dedicated to nuclear astrophysics'' by K. Setoodehnia, R. Longland, C. Marshall, F. P. Chaves, K. Kowal, & C. Seed|title=[[Nuclei in the Cosmos|Proceedings of the 14th International Symposium on Nuclei in the Cosmos (NIC2016)]]|pages=021102 (3 pages)|doi=10.7566/JPSCP.14.021102}}</ref>

==Biography==
Enge completed his secondary education in 1940 in [[Bodø (town)|Bodø]]. He studied electrical engineering and received in 1947 his engineering degree from the [[Norwegian Institute of Technology]] (now part of the [[Norwegian University of Science and Technology]]). He married his first wife in 1947.<ref name=interview>{{cite web|title=Interview of Harald Enge by Jan Vaagen on 1987 August 6|website=Niels Bohr Library & Archives, American Institute of Physics|date=15 January 2015 |url=http://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/4591}}</ref> From 1948 to 1955 he was a research associate and lecturer in physics at the [[University of Bergen]].<ref name=aip/> For a year and a half in 1950 and 1951, he worked at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). For four months he was supported by MIT's Foreign Students Summer Program and then was given a salaried job by William Weber Buechner (1914–1985).<ref name=interview/><ref>{{cite journal|date=October 1985|volume=38|issue=10|pages=132–133|doi=10.1063/1.2814749|title=Obituary. William Weber Buechner|author=Enge, Harald A.|journal=Physics Today|doi-access=free}}</ref> At MIT Enge did research in nuclear physics using a magnetic spectrograph while working with the team led by [[Robert J. Van de Graaff]]. During this time at MIT, Enge also designed his first broad-range spectrograph, which he built when he returned to the University of Bergen.<ref name=PT1984/><ref>{{cite journal|author=Vaagen, Jan S.|year=2008|title= Obituary. Harald A. Enge|journal=Nuclear Physics News|volume=8|issue=3|page=43|doi=10.1080/10506890802336471|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 1954 he received his doctorate from the University of Bergen. His dissertation was supervised by [[Bjørn Trumpy]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Harald A. Enge|website=PhysicsTree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=215321}}</ref>

In the MIT physics department, Enge was an instructor from 1955 to 1956, an assistant professor from 1956 to 1959, an associate professor from 1959 to 1963, and a full professor from 1963 to 1986, when he retired as professor emeritus.<ref name=aip>{{cite web|title=Harald A. Enge, Biography|website=American Institute of Physics|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11508010.html}}</ref> He became a U.S. citizen.<ref name=interview/>

He was, for many years, the director of the MIT research group started by Robert J. Van de Graaff and was an internationally recognized expert on the design of [[magnetic spectrometer]]s.<ref name=obitBostonGlobe/> Enge held multiple patents in various fields including magnetic and electric optics, [[Particle accelerator|accelerator]]s, power supplies and [[Isotope separation|mass separator]]s.<ref>{{cite news|title=Obituary. Harald A. Enge, retired physics professor, 87|date=April 30, 2008|newspaper=MIT News|url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2008/obit-enge-tt0430.html}}</ref>

In 1967 he was co-founder and chair of Deuteron Inc. He was also associated with the Deltaray Corporation (1969 to 1973) and the Gammaray Corporation (1981).<ref name=interview/>

He received in 1984 the [[Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics]] for his work in the field of nuclear physics.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tom W. Prize in Nuclear Physics Recipient, Harald A. Enge|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Enge&first_nm=Harald&year=1984}}</ref>

In 1985 he received an honorary doctorate from the University of Bergen.<ref name=interview/>

His first wife died in 1988. Upon his death in 2008, he was survived by his second wife, three sons from his first marriage, seven grandchildren, and five great-grandchildren.<ref name=obitBostonGlobe/>
